depth/ask: Ask a language model for seventeen times twenty four, and make it answer at once. Here it says four hundred and eighteen: wrong.
depth/pass: To write each token, the model runs once through its stack of layers. That run is called a pass, and every pass goes through the same layers, so one pass can do only so much.
depth/depth: Answering at once, the whole product has to be worked out inside that single pass.
depth/paper: On paper, you would write down a middle result, and build on it.
depth/step1: So ask the model to write its steps first. Now the first pass has one small step: seventeen times twenty is three hundred and forty.
depth/feed: Each token it writes joins the text, and the next pass reads it. So that pass starts from three hundred and forty, and takes the next step: seventeen times four is sixty eight.
depth/answer: The third pass adds them: four hundred and eight, right. No pass did more than one small step.
depth/same: The model never changed: same layers, same weights. Only the number of passes grew.
depth/name: Steps written out before the answer like this are called a chain of thought: each step a link, hooked onto the last.
roots/nye: In 2021, Maxwell Nye and colleagues saw language models do well at tasks done in one pass, and struggle with ones that take many steps, like adding long numbers.
roots/scratch: They trained models to write the steps on a scratchpad first, like your paper, and the models got far better.
roots/prompt: In 2022, Jason Wei and colleagues at Google needed no special training. They put a few worked examples, steps and all, in the prompt: the text the model is given to continue.
roots/named: A large enough model then wrote steps of its own. They called them a chain of thought, since they mimic thinking step by step toward an answer.
roots/kojima: Months later, Takeshi Kojima and colleagues dropped even the examples, and added one sentence: let's think step by step.
roots/gain: On arithmetic word problems, that took one model from seventeen point seven percent right to seventy eight point seven percent.
roots/order: The steps must come first: each position sees only what came before it, so steps after the answer come too late.
cost/tokens: Those steps cost tokens. Answering at once, the model wrote two. With its steps, thirty more came first, then the same two-token answer.
cost/ms: Each token is one more pass, and each pass takes about the same time: say twenty milliseconds. So two tokens take forty.
cost/slow: With its steps, it is thirty two tokens: thirty two times twenty, six hundred and forty milliseconds.
cost/ratio: Sixteen times as long, just as thirty two tokens is sixteen times two: with equal time per token, times compare like token counts.
cost/extra: Both end with the same answer, so the extra time is just the steps: thirty tokens, six hundred milliseconds.
cost/long: Two thousand tokens of steps take forty thousand milliseconds: forty seconds before the answer begins.
budget/budget: Turn it around. Say the reply must be done within two seconds: that is two thousand milliseconds.
budget/fit: At twenty milliseconds a token, two thousand over twenty is a hundred tokens in all.
budget/left: If the answer itself needs twenty of them, the steps get at most eighty.
budget/helps: So spend tokens on steps when the answer is built from them: arithmetic, a word problem, anything where each step needs the last.
budget/recall: Ask for the capital of France, and there is nothing to build on. The model knows it or it does not, and the steps only cost time.
